nameStory: The 'corporal' name comes from military terminology, referring to this dragonfly's tendency to patrol a specific territory like a soldier on duty. The 'blue' part describes the mature male's powdery blue coloration that develops as he ages, transforming from his youthful brown and yellow pattern into his distinguished blue uniform.
description: The Blue Corporal is a medium-sized dragonfly that's one of our most common skimmers in New England. Males start life with brown and yellow markings but mature into a striking powder-blue color with dark wing bases. Females keep their brown and yellow pattern throughout life. They're active patrol fliers that often return to the same perch repeatedly, making them easier to observe than many other dragonflies.

idTips.label: Male's powder-blue body
idTips.description: Mature males develop a chalky, powder-blue coating over their entire abdomen and thorax that looks almost dusty to the touch, completely masking their original brown pattern

idTips.label: Dark wing bases
idTips.description: Both sexes have distinctive dark brown or black patches at the base of all four wings, creating a bold contrast against the clear wing tips

idTips.label: Perching behavior
idTips.description: Often returns to the same favorite perch on a stick, rock, or bare ground, sitting horizontally with wings spread wide like most skimmers

idTips.label: Female's brown and yellow pattern
idTips.description: Females retain their intricate brown body with bright yellow spots and stripes throughout life, never developing the male's blue coloration

idTips.label: Medium size
idTips.description: Noticeably smaller than the large darners but bigger than the dainty dancers, with a robust, stocky build typical of skimmers

habitat: Blue Corporals frequent sunny areas around ponds, lakes, slow streams, and marshes throughout New England. They prefer waters with muddy or sandy bottoms and nearby open areas for hunting, often seen patrolling forest clearings and meadows adjacent to water. Look for them perching on bare ground, rocks, or low vegetation in full sunlight.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging in late May, with young males still showing their brown and yellow juvenile coloration before developing their blue powder coating.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity from June through August when mature blue males are most visible patrolling territories and mating occurs frequently.
seasonality.fall: Activity continues into September with some individuals persisting into early October, though numbers decline significantly after the first frost.
seasonality.winter: No adults present; the species overwinters as nymphs (juvenile stage) in pond and lake sediments, developing underwater until the next spring emergence.

funFact: Male Blue Corporals undergo one of the most dramatic color transformations in the dragonfly world - they literally dust themselves with a waxy blue powder called pruinescence that completely changes their appearance from brown-and-yellow youngsters into powder-blue adults, like a natural costume change!
confusionNotes: Young male Blue Corporals before they turn blue can be tricky to distinguish from females, but males have slightly broader abdomens and different clasper shapes at the tail tip. The dark wing bases help separate them from other brown dragonflies in the area.
contextualKnowledge: The scientific name 'deplanata' means 'flattened,' referring to the somewhat flattened shape of this dragonfly's abdomen. Despite being called 'little corporal' in some regions, they're actually medium-sized among New England dragonflies - not particularly small.
compareHints: Blue Corporals are the most common of the three corporal species in New England. Chalk-fronted Corporals have a distinctive white face and shoulder stripes, while White Corporals develop an overall whitish pruinescence rather than blue. The dark wing bases are shared by all corporals, making this a reliable family trait to look for.

relatedSpecies.distinction: The Chalk-fronted Corporal differs from its corporal cousins by that distinctive white "chalk" on mature males—White Corporals have white markings in different places, while Blue Corporals develop blue pruinescence instead.

Among the three Corporal species in New England, the White Corporal is distinguished by its all-over chalky white coating on mature males, compared to the Chalk-fronted Corporal's bright white face with blue-gray body, and the Blue Corporal's more uniformly blue-gray pruinescence.
